To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bis-POC derivatives of PMEA and PMPA hydrolyze at a rate comparable to their mono-POC analogs and are stable at pH 7 and 25 °C for several days.
bis-POC prodrugs of PMPA and PMEA hydrolyze via P-O bond cleavage at physiological pH values.
bis-POC prodrug hydrolysis is a pH-dependent reaction that is catalyzed by both acid and base.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel prodrugs of the anti-HIV nucleoside analogs PMEA (adefovir dipivoxil) and PMPA (tenofovir) which are currently used in the treatment of HIV/AIDS.
the development of novel antivirals for the treatment of HIV infection.
the synthesis and study of the kinetics of degradation of the oxy-carbonyloxy-methyl prodrugs of tenofovir (PMEA) and adefovir (PMPA) in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bis-POC prodrugs of PMEA and PMPA are stable at pH 7 in the presence of 50% DMSO and 50% aqueous buffer.
hydrolysis proceeds by the same pathway as for the mono-POC derivatives.
bis-POC esters of PMEA and PMPA undergo hydrolysis in solution primarily via P-O bond cleavage with the corresponding monoesters being the only observable degradation products.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hydrolysis of the bis-POC prodrugs of PMEA and PMPA proceeds via P-O bond cleavage with a minor pathway via C-O bond cleavage.
bis-POC prodrugs of PMEA and PMPA were shown to be stable at pH 4.0 but hydrolyzed rapidly above pH 7.
the degradation of both bis-POC esters proceeds via a P-O bond cleavage with a small contribution from C-O bond cleavage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the POC esters of PMEA and PMPA are more stable in aqueous solution at neutral pH than the corresponding mono-esters.
the POC esters of PMEA and PMPA can be used for in vivo delivery of the corresponding nucleoside analogs, PME and PMP.
bis-POC esters of PMEA and PMPA can be used as prodrugs to achieve sustained release of the parent drug in vivo.
